name: Impostor syndrome
statement: High achievers who cannot internalise their success believe they have fooled everyone, and expect to be found out as frauds.
meaning: The claim is about a gap between the record and the self-image. Someone holds degrees, promotions and praise, and reads every one of them as luck, charm, timing or an administrative error. Clance and Imes described four behaviours that maintain the belief once it is in place: diligence and hard work, intellectual flattery, using charm to win over a mentor whose approval is then discounted, and holding on to the impostor position to avoid what they took to be the social penalties on a confident woman. A woman may participate in one or more of these behaviours, they write, but seldom all of them. The belief is self-sealing, because each new success is explained away by the same machinery that explained the last one. What the term does not describe is a disorder. Bravata and colleagues state that impostor syndrome is not featured in the American Psychiatric Association's Diagnostic and Statistical Manual and is not listed as a diagnosis in ICD-10, and they recommend that it be considered for inclusion in the DSM.

origin.who: Pauline Rose Clance and Suzanne Imes
origin.note: The paper is a clinical report, not an experiment. It opens by describing five years of individual psychotherapy, theme-centred groups and college classes with over 150 highly successful women. Across its six pages it reports no measurement, no comparison group and no test statistic. The word 'syndrome' does not appear in it. The title spells the word 'imposter'; the body of the paper spells it 'impostor'.

evidence: Clance and Imes list the groups their observations came from: 95 undergraduate women and 10 PhD faculty women at a private Midwestern college, 15 undergraduates, 20 graduate students and 10 faculty at a large southern urban university, six medical students, and 22 professional women in law, anthropology, nursing, social work and other fields. Those numbers sum to 178, against the 'over 150' in the text. Approximately one-third were therapy clients; the rest were in growth-oriented interaction groups or classes taught by the authors. All were women, primarily white and middle to upper class, aged 20 to 45. A footnote reports the authors' clinical impression that the phenomenon occurs with much less frequency and much less intensity in men, and says the observation needs to be researched. Measurement arrived later. Clance published the 20-item Impostor Test in her 1985 book, and the copy reprinted on her own site carries her scoring bands: 40 or less means few impostor characteristics, 41 to 60 moderate, 61 to 80 frequent, and above 80 intense. Chrisman and colleagues compared the scale with the Perceived Fraudulence Scale in 1995, found three components they named Fake, Discount and Luck, and reported that impostor feelings were related to but discriminable from depression, self-esteem, social anxiety and self-monitoring. Their sample is given as 269 undergraduates in Mak, Kleitman and Abbott's review table, which is where this entry read it, the paper itself being closed at the publisher. Mak and colleagues appraised 18 validation studies covering four scales in 2019 and found the position weaker than its use suggests. The Clance scale, the Harvey Impostor Scale and the Perceived Fraudulence Scale rest on multidimensional definitions of the construct yet calculate overall total scores and define no subscale scores, which their review says appears to contradict the theoretical conceptualisation. It is premature, they conclude, to select a gold standard measure.

replication.headline: The correlates reproduce, including across two independent meta-analyses that agree closely, and the prevalence claim does not: the widely quoted 70% traces to a newspaper feature, while Bravata's review puts prevalence anywhere between 9% and 82% depending on the cutoff.
replication.detail: Bravata and colleagues searched Medline, Embase and PsycINFO from January 1966 to May 2018 and found 66 articles describing 62 studies with 14,161 participants, 60% of them women. Prevalence ran 'from 9 to 82% largely depending on the screening tool and cutoff used'. Their sharpest illustration is a single sample: Chae and colleagues' Korean Catholics gave 39% at a scale cutoff of 58 and 24% at a cutoff of 62. That study's size is 654 in Bravata's table and 640 in Mak's, and the original is closed at the publisher, so the discrepancy stands unresolved here. None of the included articles presented an evaluation of a specific treatment. Omar and colleagues pooled 34 studies of 9,550 medical students and report prevalence of 49%, 95% CI 43% to 54%, with I-squared of 95.6%, P < 0.001. Females came out at 51% against males at 40%, P = 0.021. Their abstract holds that the variance driven by different measurement tools 'suggests that researchers may not be consistently measuring the same construct', and that reliance on unvalidated cutoffs further weakens the validity of prevalence estimates. The associations hold up better than the counts. Rohrmann, Bechtoldt and Leonhardt had 457 people open their online study, 252 begin it and 242 remain after excluding those without leadership responsibility. Correlations rest on between 183 and 242 of them, because of pairwise deletion. The model that kept impostor feelings as a separate factor fitted better than each of five models merging it with concern over mistakes, neuroticism, depression, apprehension or core self-evaluations: CFI 0.948 against 0.921 for the closest rival. Their strongest correlation was 0.57 with concern over mistakes and doubts, against 0.48 for neuroticism, 0.48 for apprehensiveness and -0.46 for core self-evaluations. Fleischhauer and colleagues drew 209 completed responses from 448 accesses, 79% of them from women, and report r = -0.71 with self-esteem and r = 0.62 with neuroticism. Two meta-analyses then took the perfectionism link apart, and landed in the same place. Hill and Gotwals followed a preregistered protocol, pooled 25 studies with 12,141 participants and 42 effect sizes, and report perfectionistic strivings at r+ = 0.15, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.23, I-squared 91.79, against perfectionistic concerns at r+ = 0.61, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.65, I-squared 92.55. Breit and colleagues pooled 26 records and 91 effect sizes and report reliability-adjusted Fisher's z of .159, 95% CI .051 to .268, for strivings, and .747, 95% CI .632 to .863, for concerns, which they convert to correlations of .16 and .63. Partialled out, strivings show no unique relationship, z = -.07, 95% CI -.18 to .04, p = .194. Both meta-analyses carry heterogeneity above 90%, and Breit's prediction interval for strivings runs from -0.35 to 0.67. The 70% claim has a shorter trail. Sakulku and Alexander's review writes that 'it is estimated that 70% of people will experience at least one episode of this Impostor Phenomenon in their lives', citing Gravois (2007), a Chronicle of Higher Education feature. ERIC's record of that feature says Clance teamed up with Gail Matthews in the mid-1980s to conduct a survey, and that they found about 70 percent of people from all walks of life have felt like impostors for at least some part of their careers. Bravata's table records the published Matthews and Clance paper of 1985 as 41 people with prevalence not stated. Neither ERIC's record nor Bravata's table of 62 studies attaches 70% to a measured prevalence, and a Crossref search of Clance's impostor publications from 1980 to 1990 returns two scale records and the Matthews paper, with no survey report among them.

study.cite: Bravata, D. M., Watts, S. A., Keefer, A. L., Madhusudhan, D. K., Taylor, K. T., Clark, D. M., Nelson, R. S., Cokley, K. O., & Hagg, H. K. (2020). Prevalence, predictors, and treatment of impostor syndrome: A systematic review. Journal of General Internal Medicine, 35(4), 1252-1275.

limits: There is no original experiment to repeat, so 'replication' here means whether later measurement recovers what the 1978 paper described. It partly does. Two figures rest on documents this entry could not open. The Gravois feature sits behind the Chronicle's paywall, whose article page returned a challenge page rather than the text, so the 70% sentence is read from Sakulku and Alexander's PDF and from ERIC's record EJ782339. Chrisman and colleagues' paper is closed at the publisher with no repository copy in Unpaywall, so its sample size is quoted from Mak's table. Omar and colleagues' meta-analysis is licensed CC-BY, and Springer's article and PDF endpoints both returned a bot challenge to this session, so its figures come from the publisher abstract as served by Europe PMC and PubMed. Chae and colleagues' Korean study is closed, which is why the 654 against 640 discrepancy above is left standing rather than settled. The prevalence literature is also skewed young: Bravata reports a weighted mean age of 20 years, with 34 of the included studies drawn from students. Searches covered Crossref, DataCite, PubMed, Europe PMC, PMC, Unpaywall, OpenAlex, ERIC, Frontiers, Springer, Wiley, Hogrefe, Ovid, ScienceDirect and general web search.
misreadings: The 70% figure is the main one, and it is quoted as though a survey report produced it rather than a magazine paragraph about one. The second is the word 'syndrome', which Clance and Imes did not use and which implies a clinical category that neither the DSM nor ICD-10 contains. Gullifor and colleagues counted what the workplace literature calls it: phenomenon in 69.1% of 188 documents, syndrome in 35.6%. Feenstra and colleagues argue for keeping 'phenomenon' on the ground that 'syndrome' implies a medical model of dysfunction within the individual, and that the environment does part of the work. A third misreading treats a questionnaire score above some cutoff as a diagnosis. The same Korean sample is 39% impostors or 24% impostors depending on which cutoff is chosen, and neither 58 nor 62 is one of Clance's own bands, which break at 40, 60 and 80. The last is that it is a women's condition. That is what the 1978 sample was, by construction, and Bravata found impostor syndrome common among both men and women, from adolescents to late-stage professionals.
